'''Leroy "Lee" Edward Hood''' (born October 10, 1938) is an American [[biologist]] who has served on the faculties at the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech) and the [[University of Washington]].<ref name="Kyoto">{{cite web|title=Leroy Edward Hood|url=http://www.kyotoprize.org/en/laureates/leroy_edward_hood/|website=Kyoto Prize|access-date=31 May 2017}}</ref> His inventions include the first gas phase [[protein sequencer]] (1982), for determining the sequence of amino acids in a given protein;<ref name="Weingart"/><ref name="Vanderkam"/> a [[DNA synthesis|DNA synthesizer]] (1983), to synthesize short sections of DNA;<ref name="Weingart"/><ref name="Stephenson"/> a [[peptide synthesizer]] (1984), to combine amino acids into longer peptides and short proteins;<ref name="Vanderkam">{{cite news|last1=Vanderkam|first1=Laura|title=Any knowledge that might be useful: Leroy Hood|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/any-knowledge-leroy-hood/|access-date=2 June 2017|work=Scientific American|date=June 16, 2008}}</ref><ref name="Personal"/> the first automated [[DNA sequencer]] (1986), to identify the order of nucleotides in DNA;<ref name="Kyoto"/><ref name="Hutchison"/><ref name="NAS2017"/> ink-jet [[oligonucleotide]] technology for synthesizing DNA<ref name="IEEEAward"/><ref name="Hamadeh">{{cite book|editor-last1=Hamadeh|editor-first1=Hisham K.|editor-last2=Afshari|editor-first2=Cynthia A.|title=Toxicogenomics: principles and applications|date=2004|publisher=Wiley-Liss|location=Hoboken, NJ|isbn=978-0-471-43417-7|page=50|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9orajdYNM10C&pg=PA50|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> and nanostring technology for analyzing single molecules of DNA and RNA.<ref name="ISB">{{cite web|title=Leroy Hood, MD, PhD|url=https://www.systemsbiology.org/bio/leroy-hood/|website=Institute for Systems Biology|access-date=31 May 2017}}</ref><ref name="Moore">{{cite news|last1=Moore|first1=Charles|title=MD Anderson and NanoString Technologies To Jointly Develop Multi-Omic Assays Simultaneously Profiling Gene and Protein Expression|url=https://bionews-tx.com/news/2015/04/07/md-anderson-and-nanostring-technologies-to-jointly-develop-multi-omic-assays-simultaneously-profiling-gene-and-protein-expression/|access-date=2 June 2017|work=Bio News Texas|date=April 7, 2015|archive-date=10 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160410030300/https://bionews-tx.com/news/2015/04/07/md-anderson-and-nanostring-technologies-to-jointly-develop-multi-omic-assays-simultaneously-profiling-gene-and-protein-expression/}}</ref> 
 
The protein sequencer, DNA synthesizer, peptide synthesizer, and DNA sequencer were commercialized through [[Applied Biosystems|Applied Biosystems, Inc.]]<ref name="Haugen"/> and the ink-jet technology was commercialized through [[Agilent Technologies]].<ref name="IEEEAward"/><ref name="Hamadeh"/> The automated DNA sequencer was an enabling technology for the [[Human Genome Project]].<ref name="Hutchison"/> The peptide synthesizer was used in the synthesis of the [[HIV-1 protease|HIV protease]] by [[Stephen Kent (chemist)|Stephen Kent]] and others, and the development of a [[Protease inhibitor (pharmacology)|protease inhibitor]] for [[AIDS]] treatment.<ref name="Personal">{{cite journal|last1=Hood|first1=Leroy|title=A Personal View of Molecular Technology and How It Has Changed Biology|journal=Journal of Proteome Research|date=October 2002|volume=1|issue=5|pages=399–409|doi=10.1021/pr020299f|pmid=12645911|url=http://lazowska.cs.washington.edu/initiatives/JPR.pdf|access-date=1 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="protease">{{cite journal|title=Active HIV protease analog synthesized chemically|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=27 February 1995|volume=73|issue=9|page=38|doi=10.1021/cen-v073n009.p038}}</ref><ref name="Schneider">{{cite journal|last1=Schneider|first1=Jens|last2=Kent|first2=Stephen B.H.|title=Enzymatic activity of a synthetic 99 residue protein corresponding to the putative HIV-1 protease|journal=Cell|date=July 1988|volume=54|issue=3|pages=363–368|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(88)90199-7|pmid=3293801|s2cid=46170353|url=http://www.cell.com/cell/pdf/0092-8674(88)90199-7.pdf|access-date=1 June 2017}}</ref>

Hood established the first cross-disciplinary biology department, the Department of Molecular Biotechnology (MBT), at the University of Washington in 1992,<ref name="Gardiner"/><ref name="NAS2017"/> and co-founded the [[Institute for Systems Biology]] in 2000.<ref name="ISB"/> Hood is credited with introducing the term "[[systems biology]]",<ref name="Rau"/> and advocates for "P4 medicine", medicine that is "predictive, [[Personalized medicine|personalized]], preventive, and participatory."<ref name="Kistler"/><ref name="Carlson">{{cite journal|last1=Carlson|first1=Bob|title=P4 Medicine Could Transform Healthcare, but Payers and Physicians Are Not Yet Convinced|journal=Biotechnology Healthcare|date=2010|volume=7|issue=3|pages=7–8|pmc=2957728|pmid=22478823}}</ref> ''[[Scientific American]]'' counted him among the 10 most influential people in the field of biotechnology in 2015.<ref name="WorldView">{{cite news|title=The WorldView 100: Who are the most influential people in Biotech today?|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/wv/assets/2015_SAWorldView.pdf|access-date=2 June 2017|work=Scientific American WorldView: A Global Biotechnology Perspective|page=5,10–11|date=2015|archive-date=9 February 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160209135659/http://www.scientificamerican.com/wv/assets/2015_SAWorldView.pdf}}</ref>

Hood was elected a member of the [[National Academy of Engineering]] in 2007 for the invention and commercialization of key instruments, notably the automated DNA sequencer, that have enabled the biotechnology revolution.

==Early life==
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | headerimage=  |video1= [https://tedxseattle.com/talks/future-of-medicine/ Leroy Hood: Future of Medicine], TedX Rainier | video2 = [https://www.systemsbiology.org/news/2012/11/08/profiles-of-innovation-lee-hood-at-northeastern-university/ Profiles of Innovation: Lee Hood at Northeastern University] | video3 = [https://ieeetv.ieee.org/ieee-products/2014-medal-for-innovations-in-healthcare-technology 2014 Medal for Innovations in Healthcare Technology], IEEE.tv }}

Hood was born on October 10, 1938, in [[Missoula, Montana]], to Thomas Edward Hood and Myrtle Evylan Wadsworth.<ref name="Sleeman"/> and grew up in [[Shelby, Montana|Shelby]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Vanderkam|first=Laura|title=Any knowledge that might be useful: Leroy Hood|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/any-knowledge-leroy-hood/|access-date=2023-02-10|website=Scientific American|language=en}}</ref> His father was an [[electrical engineer]], and his mother had a degree in [[home economics]]. Hood was one of four children, including a sister and two brothers, including a brother with [[Down syndrome]]. One of his grandfathers was a rancher and ran a summer geology camp for university students, which Hood attended as a high school student. Hood excelled in math and science, being one of forty students nationally to win a [[Westinghouse Science Talent Search]].<ref name=KyotoLecture2002>{{cite web|last1=Hood |first1=Leroy |title=My Life and Adventures Integrating Biology and Technology: A Commemorative Lecture for the 2002 Kyoto Prize in Advanced Technologies |url=https://www.systemsbiology.org/download/2002Kyoto.pdf |website=Systems Biology |access-date=1 December 2016 |url-status=bot: unknown |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120716225254/https://www.systemsbiology.org/download/2002Kyoto.pdf |archive-date=16 July 2012 }}</ref> In addition, Hood played several high school sports and debate, the latter of which he would credit for his success in science communication later in his career.<ref name=":0" />

==Education==
Hood received his undergraduate education from the [[California Institute of Technology]] (Caltech), where his professors included notables such as [[Richard Feynman]]<ref name="Rau">{{cite journal|last1=Rau|first1=Marlene|last2=Wegener|first2=Anna-Lynn|last3=Furtado|first3=Sonia|title=New approaches to old systems: interview with Leroy Hood|journal=Science in School|date=2009|issue=12|pages=14–18|url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/e020/c4b90f61542555e8d42b5ab497f1c7c39151.pdf|access-date=31 May 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171212084239/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/e020/c4b90f61542555e8d42b5ab497f1c7c39151.pdf|archive-date=12 December 2017}}</ref> and [[Linus Pauling]].<ref name="Haugen">{{cite book|last1=Haugen|first1=Peter|title=Biology: decade by decade|date=2007|publisher=Facts On File|location=New York|isbn=978-0-8160-5530-2|page=216|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rLnRflswhHcC&pg=PA216|access-date=31 May 2017}}</ref><ref name="KyotoLecture2002"/> Hood received an [[Doctor of Medicine|MD]] from [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine]] in 1964 and a [[PhD]] from Caltech in 1968,<ref name="Smithsonian">{{cite web|title=DNA Sequencing (RU 9549)|url=http://siarchives.si.edu/research/videohistory_catalog9549.html|website=Smithsonian Institution Archives|access-date=2 June 2017|archive-date=26 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170926142903/http://siarchives.si.edu/research/videohistory_catalog9549.html}}</ref> where he worked with [[William J. Dreyer]] on antibody diversity.<ref name="Gardiner"/> Dreyer is credited with giving Hood two important pieces of advice:  "If you want to practice biology, do it on the leading edge, and if you want to be on the leading edge, invent new tools for deciphering biological information."<ref name="Hall">{{cite book|last1=Hall|first1=Bronwyn H.|last2=Rosenberg|first2=Nathan|title=Handbook of the economics of innovation.|date=2010|publisher=Elsevier/North Holland|location=Amsterdam|isbn=978-0-08-093111-1|page=229|edition=1st|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4nZTCD_zjN4C&pg=PA229|access-date=4 June 2017}}</ref>

==Career==
[[File:Leroy Hood 1986.png|thumb|left|Hood in 1986]]

In 1967, Hood joined the [[National Institutes of Health]] (NIH), to work in the immunology branch of the [[National Cancer Institute]] as a senior investigator.<ref name="Yount">{{cite book|last1=Yount|first1=Lisa|title=A to Z of biologists|date=2003|publisher=Facts on File|location=New York|isbn=978-0-8160-4541-9|pages=132–134|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pOdHrsTZ-RYC&pg=PA132|access-date=15 June 2017}}</ref>

In 1970, he returned to Caltech as an [[assistant professor]].<ref name="Gardiner"/> He was promoted to [[associate professor]] in 1973, [[full professor]] in 1975, and was named Bowles Professor of Biology in 1977. He served as chairman of the Division of Biology from 1980-1989 and director of Caltech's Special Cancer Center in 1981.<ref name="Sleeman">{{cite book|last1=Sleeman|first1=Elizabeth|title=The international who's who 2004|date=2003|publisher=Europa|location=London|isbn=978-1-85743-217-6|page=750|edition=67|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=sR4Ch1dMe8IC&pg=PA750|access-date=3 June 2017}}</ref>

Hood has been a leader and a proponent of [[Interdisciplinarity|cross-disciplinary research]] in chemistry and biology.<ref name="Gardiner">{{cite news|last1=Gardiner|first1=Mary Beth|title=Leroy Hood: Discovery Science Biotech guru Leroy Hood leads researchers in a new direction|url=http://www.mc.vanderbilt.edu/lens/article/?id=203&pg=999|access-date=2 June 2017|work=Lens: A New Way of Looking at Science|date=2003}}</ref> 
In 1989 he stepped down as chairman of the Division of Biology to create and become director of a newly funded [[National Science Foundation|NSF]] Science and Technology Center at Caltech.<ref name="NSF9214821">{{cite web|title=Award Abstract #9214821 Science & Technology Center for Molecular Biotechnology|url=https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=9214821|website=National Science Foundation|date=November 24, 1999}}</ref> The NSF Center for the Development of an Integrated Protein and Nucleic Acid Biotechnology became one of the founding research centers of the [[Beckman Institute at Caltech]] in 1989.<ref name="Beckman">{{cite journal|title=Beckman Institute becomes concrete|journal=Engineering & Science|date=1989|issue=Spring|pages=22–34|url=http://calteches.library.caltech.edu/3608/1/Beckman.pdf|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="hundred">{{cite book | isbn = 978-0-941901-23-9 |author1=Arnold Thackray  |author2=Minor Myers Jr. |name-list-style=amp |others = foreword by James D. Watson. | year = 2000 | publisher = Chemical Heritage Foundation | location = Philadelphia, Pa. | title = Arnold O. Beckman: one hundred years of excellence}}</ref> By this time, Hood's laboratory included more than 100 researchers, a much larger group than was usual at Caltech. A relatively small school, Caltech was not well-suited to the creation of the type of large interdisciplinary research organization that Hood sought.<ref name="Economist"/>

In October 1991, Hood announced that he would move to the University of Washington at Seattle, to found and direct the first cross-disciplinary biology department, the Department of Molecular Biotechnology (MBT) at the [[University of Washington]] Medical School.<ref name="Gardiner"/><ref name="NAS2017"/> The new department was financed by a US $12-million gift from [[Bill Gates]], who shared Hood's interest in combining biological research and computer technology and applying them to medical research.<ref name=Dietrich1992>{{cite news|last=Dietrich|first=Bill|title=Future Perfect -- Thanks To Bill Gates' $12-Million Endowment, Scientist Leroy Hood Continues His Search For A New Genetic Destiny|url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/19920209/1474735/future-perfect|access-date=17 March 2012|newspaper=The Seattle Times|date=9 February 1992}}</ref><ref name="Herring">{{cite news|last1=Herring|first1=Angela|title=Biology is a complex matter|url=http://www.northeastern.edu/news/2012/11/leroy-hood/|access-date=1 December 2016|work=News @ Northwestern|date=November 6, 2012|archive-date=1 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161201213312/http://www.northeastern.edu/news/2012/11/leroy-hood/}}</ref> [[Roger M. Perlmutter|Roger Perlmutter]], who had worked in Hood's lab at Caltech before moving to UW as chair of the immunology department, played a key role organizing his recruitment to UW.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Timmerman|first=Luke D.|title=Hood: Trailblazer of the Genomic Age|others=Tracy Cutchlow, Robert Simison|year=2016|isbn=978-0-9977093-0-8|location=[Place of publication not identified]|pages=235–240, 7, 31|oclc=959626112}}</ref> Hood and other scientists from Caltech's NSF center moved to the University of Washington during 1992-1994, where they received renewed support from the NSF as the Center for Molecular Biotechnology.<ref name="NSF9214821"/><ref name="Hanson">{{cite book|last1=Hanson|first1=Susan L.|last2=Lindee|first2=M. Susan|last3=Speaker|first3=Elizabeth|title=A guide to the Human Genome Project: technologies, people, and institutions|date=1993|publisher=Chemical Heritage Foundation|location=Philadelphia, PA|isbn=978-0-941901-10-9|page=30|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IWr15gWQED4C&pg=PA30|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> (Later, in 2001, the department of molecular biotechnology and the genetics department at UW reorganized to form the department of genome sciences.<ref>{{cite web|title=Collaborative Science Reveals Genome Secrets|url=http://www.gs.washington.edu/about/history/genome_sciences.pdf|website=Genome Sciences, University of Washington|access-date=3 June 2017}}</ref>)

In 2000 Hood resigned his position at the University of Washington to become co-founder and president of the non-profit Institute for Systems Biology (ISB),<ref name="Pollack">{{cite news|last1=Pollack|first1=Andrew|title=SCIENTIST AT WORK: LEROY HOOD; A Biotech Superstar Looks at the Bigger Picture|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/04/17/science/scientist-at-work-leroy-hood-a-biotech-superstar-looks-at-the-bigger-picture.html|access-date=31 May 2017|work=The New York Times|date=April 17, 2001}}</ref> possibly the first independent systems biology organization.<ref name="Vermeulen">{{cite book|last1=Vermeulen|first1=Niki|title=Supersizing Science On Building Large-scale Research Projects in Biology.|date=2010|publisher=Gardners Books|isbn=978-1-59942-364-7|pages=135–136|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PzxPZwuTR2wC&pg=PA135|access-date=3 June 2017}}</ref> His co-founders were protein chemist [[Ruedi Aebersold]] and immunologist [[Alan Aderem]].<ref name="Hsiao-Ching Chou">{{cite web|author=Hsiao-Ching Chou|title=Institute for Systems Biology Recruits Technology Pioneer James Heath as President|url=https://www.systemsbiology.org/news/2017/04/03/institute-systems-biology-recruits-technology-pioneer-james-heath-president/|website=Institute for Systems Biology|access-date=April 3, 2017|date=2017-04-03}}</ref> Hood is still an affiliate professor at the University of Washington in Computer Science,<ref name="CV">{{cite web|title=DR. LEROY E. HOOD Curriculum Vitae|url=https://www.systemsbiology.org/wp-content/uploads/Hood_CV_June-2015.pdf|website=Institute for Systems Biology|access-date=3 June 2017}}</ref> Bioengineering<ref>{{cite web|title=Leroy E. Hood|url=https://bioe.uw.edu/portfolio-items/hood/|website=Department of Bioengineering|date=23 August 2013 |publisher=University of Washington School of Medicine|access-date=3 June 2017}}</ref> and Immunology.<ref>{{cite web|title=Leroy Hood, M.D., Ph.D.|url=http://immunology.washington.edu/leroy-hood-md-phd|website=Department of Immunology|publisher=University of Washington School of Medicine|access-date=3 June 2017}}</ref> In April 2017, the ISB announced that Hood will be succeeded as president of ISB as of January 2018 by [[James R. Heath|James Heath]], while continuing to lead his research group at ISB and serving on ISB's board of directors.<ref name="Hsiao-Ching Chou"/>

Hood believes that a combination of big data and systems biology has the potential to revolutionize healthcare and create a proactive medical approach focused on maximizing the [[Wellness (medicine)|wellness]] of the individual. He coined the term "P4 medicine" in 2003.<ref name="Guest">{{cite book|last1=Guest|first1=Greg|last2=Namey|first2=Emily E.|title=Public health research methods|date=2015|publisher=Sage Pubns|isbn=978-1-4522-4133-3|page=669|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1sQ_AwAAQBAJ&pg=PA669|access-date=3 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Flores">{{cite journal|last1=Hood|first1=Leroy|last2=Flores|first2=Mauricio|title=A personal view on systems medicine and the emergence of proactive P4 medicine: predictive, preventive, personalized and participatory|journal=New Biotechnology|date=September 2012|volume=29|issue=6|pages=613–624|doi=10.1016/j.nbt.2012.03.004|pmid=22450380|s2cid=873920}}</ref> 
In 2010 ISB partnered with the [[Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center]] in [[Columbus, Ohio]], to establish the nonprofit P4 Medicine Institute (P4MI). Its goal was stated as being "to lead the transformation of healthcare from a reactive system to one that predicts and prevents disease, tailors diagnosis and therapy to the individual consumer and engages patients in the active pursuit of a quantified understanding of wellness; i.e. one that is predictive, preventive, personalized and participatory (P4)."<ref name="Kirk">{{cite news|last1=Kirk|first1=Sherri L.|title=Ohio State Partners with Research Giant to Advance Health Care and Form P4 Medicine Institute|url=http://p4mi.org/ohio-state-partners-research-giant-advance-health-care-and-form-p4-medicine-institute|access-date=3 June 2017|work=P4 Medicine Institute|date=May 14, 2010|archive-date=9 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170609101251/http://www.p4mi.org/ohio-state-partners-research-giant-advance-health-care-and-form-p4-medicine-institute}}</ref> In 2012, P4 Medical Institute established an agreement with its first community health partner, [[PeaceHealth]]. PeaceHealth is a not-for-profit Catholic health care system, operating in a variety of communities in Alaska, Washington and Oregon.<ref name="PeaceHealth">{{cite news|last1=PeaceHealth|title=P4 Medicine institute, PeaceHealth Launch Partnership to Pilot New Model in Health Care|url=http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/p4-medicine-institute-peacehealth-launch-partnership-to-pilot-new-model-in-health-care-142759165.html|access-date=3 June 2017|work=PR Newswire|date=15 March 2012}}</ref><ref name="Timmerman">{{cite news|last1=Timmerman|first1=Luke|title=Lee Hood's P4 Initiative Finds Community Partner, PeaceHealth|url=http://www.xconomy.com/seattle/2012/03/15/lee-hoods-p4-medicine-institute-gets-new-partner-peacehealth/|access-date=3 June 2017|work=Xconomy|date=March 15, 2012}}</ref> In 2016, ISB affiliated with [[Providence Health & Services]],<ref name="Romano">{{cite news|last1=Romano|first1=Benjamin|title=Institute for Systems Biology, Providence Team Up for Preventive Care|url=http://www.xconomy.com/seattle/2016/03/14/institute-for-systems-biology-providence-team-up-for-preventive-care/#|access-date=4 June 2017|work=Xconomy|date=March 14, 2016}}</ref> and Hood became the senior vice president of Providence St. Joseph Health and its chief science officer.<ref name="Hsiao-Ching Chou"/>

Hood has published more than 700 peer-reviewed papers, received 36 patents, and co-authored textbooks in biochemistry, immunology, molecular biology, and genetics. In addition, he co-authored, with Daniel J. Kevles, ''The Code of Codes'', a popular book on the sequencing of the human genome.<ref name="Hutchins">{{cite web|last1=Hutchins|first1=Shawn|title=Systems biology pioneer Leroy Hood to present at inaugural lectureship|url=http://bioengineering.rice.edu/Content.aspx?id=4294967661|website=Rice University|access-date=4 June 2017}}{{Dead link|date=December 2023 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

He has been instrumental in founding 15 biotechnology companies,<ref name="ISB"/> including [[Amgen]], Applied Biosystems, Systemix, Darwin, Rosetta Inpharmatics, Integrated Diagnostics, and Accelerator Corporation.<ref name="Philippidis">{{cite news|last1=Philippidis|first1=Alex|title=Lucky 13 Serial Entrepreneurs Meet the most enterprising people in biotech|url=http://www.genengnews.com/the-lists/lucky-13-serial-entrepreneurs/77899721|access-date=4 June 2017|work=Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News|date=November 13, 2012}}</ref> In 2015, he co-founded a startup called Arivale offering a subscription-based 'scientific wellness' service<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/science/new-scientific-wellness-strategy-could-cut-chronic-illnesses-and-save-money-1.3619670|title=New 'scientific wellness' strategy could cut chronic illnesses and save money|last1=King|first1=Anthony|last2=O'Sullivan|first2=Kevin|newspaper=The Irish Times|language=en|access-date=2019-04-25}}</ref> which shut down in 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.geekwire.com/2019/scientific-wellness-startup-arivale-closes-abruptly-tragic-end-vision-transform-personal-health/|title=Scientific wellness startup Arivale closes abruptly in 'tragic' end to vision to transform personal health|date=2019-04-24|website=GeekWire|language=en-US|access-date=2019-04-25}}</ref> While praising the quality of its offering, industry commentators attributed Arivale's closure to a failure to capture sufficient [[Customer lifetime value]] to create a profit from providing the service, suggesting that insufficient numbers of customers stuck with the data-driven, personalized dietary and lifestyle coaching it provided for long enough at a price point which would make the [[business model]] work.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.seattletimes.com/business/technology/closure-of-high-tech-medical-firm-arivale-stuns-patients-i-feel-as-if-one-of-my-arms-was-cut-off/|title=Closure of high-tech medical firm Arivale stuns patients: 'I feel as if one of my arms was cut off'|date=2019-04-26|website=[[The Seattle Times]]|language=en-US|access-date=2019-06-02}}</ref>

==Research==
===Genomics and proteomics===
At Caltech, Hood and his colleagues created the technological foundation for the study of [[genomics]] and [[proteomics]] by developing five groundbreaking instruments - the protein sequencer (1982), the DNA synthesizer (1983), the peptide synthesizer (1984),<!-- Hood sometimes refers to it as a protein synthesizer -->the automated [[DNA sequencer]] (1986) and later the ink-jet DNA synthesizer.<ref name="Weingart">{{cite book|editor-last1=Weingart|editor-first1=Peter|editor-last2=Stehr|editor-first2=Nico|title=Practising interdisciplinarity|date=2000|publisher=University of Toronto press|location=Toronto|isbn=978-0-8020-8139-1|pages=237–238|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MS92DLz4gksC&pg=PA237|access-date=8 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="MIT"/><ref name="Kyoto"/><ref name="Hutchison"/><ref name="NAS2017"/>  Hood's instruments incorporated concepts of high throughput data accumulation through automation and parallelization. When applied to the study of protein and DNA chemistries, these ideas were essential to the rapid deciphering of biological information.<ref name="MIT">{{cite news|title=Rewriting Life Under Biology's Hood|work=MIT Technology Review|date=September 1, 2001|url=https://www.technologyreview.com/s/401182/under-biologys-hood/|access-date=4 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Rowen"/><ref name="revolution">{{cite web|title=Leroy Hood: There is going to be a fantastic revolution in medicine|url=http://www.laskerfoundation.org/new-noteworthy/articles/hood/|website=Albert and Mary Lasker Foundation|access-date=April 10, 2017}}</ref>

Hood had a strong interest in commercial development, actively filing patents and seeking private funding.<ref name="García-Sancho">{{cite book|last1=García-Sancho|first1=Miguel|title=Biology, computing, and the history of molecular sequencing: from proteins to DNA, 1945-2000|date=2012|publisher=Palgrave Macmillan|location=New York|isbn=978-0-230-25032-1|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A2pkfcjKk34C&pg=PT116|access-date=8 June 2017}}</ref> 
Applied Biosystems, Inc. (initially named GeneCo.) was formed in 1981 in Foster City, California, to commercialize instruments developed by Hood, Hunkapiller, Caruthers, and others.  The company was supported by venture capitalist [[William K. Bowes]], who hired Sam H. Eletr and André Marion as president and vice-president of the new company. The company shipped the first gas phase protein sequencer, Model 4790A, in August 1982. The 380 DNA synthesizer was commercialized in 1983, the 430A peptide synthesizer in 1984, and the 370A [[DNA sequencing]] system in 1986.<ref name="LSF">{{cite journal|title=The GeneCo Business Plan|journal=LSF Magazine|date=2014|volume=Winter|pages=14–15|url=https://issuu.com/lifesciencesfoundation/docs/2014.1.lsfmagwinter|access-date=8 June 2017|archive-date=5 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170905063017/https://issuu.com/lifesciencesfoundation/docs/2014.1.lsfmagwinter}}</ref><ref name="Stephenson">{{cite web|last1=Stephenson|first1=Frank|title=Twenty-five years of advancing science|url=http://home.appliedbiosystems.com/about/presskit/pdfs/25_years_advancing_science.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180329064659/http://home.appliedbiosystems.com/about/presskit/pdfs/25_years_advancing_science.pdf|archive-date=2018-03-29|website=Applied Biosystems|date=2006}}</ref>

These new instruments had a major impact on the emerging fields of proteomics and genomics.<ref name="Weingart"/><ref name="Patterson">{{cite journal|last1=Patterson|first1=Scott D.|last2=Aebersold|first2=Ruedi H.|title=Proteomics: the first decade and beyond|journal=Nature Genetics|date=March 2003|volume=33|issue=3s|pages=311–323|doi=10.1038/ng1106|pmid=12610541|s2cid=9800076}}</ref> 
The gas-liquid phase protein sequencer was developed with Michael W. Hunkapiller, then a 
research fellow at Caltech.<ref name="Smithsonian"/><ref name="Kinter"/>  The instrument makes use of the chemical process known as the [[Edman degradation]], devised by [[Pehr Edman]].<ref name="Kinter"/> Edman and Begg's 1967 design involves placing a protein or peptide sample into a spinning cup in a temperature controlled chamber. Reagents are added to cleave the protein one amino acid at the time, followed by solvents to allow extraction of reagents and byproducts. A series of analysis cycles is performed to identify a sequence, one cycle for each amino acid, and the cycle times were lengthy.<ref name="Lundblad">{{cite book|last1=Lundblad|first1=Roger L.|title=Techniques in protein modification.|date=1995|publisher=CRC Press|location=Boca Raton, Flor.|isbn=978-0-8493-2606-6|pages=40–41|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HUKWXgCKTXAC&pg=PA48}}</ref> Hood and Hunkapiller made a number of modifications, further automating steps in the analysis and improving effectiveness and shortening cycle time. By applying reagents in the gas phase instead of the liquid phase, the retention of the sample during the analysis and the sensitivity of the instrument were increased.<ref name="Kinter"/> 
[[Polybrene]] was used as a substrate coating to better anchor proteins and peptides,<ref name="Hugli">{{cite book|last1=Hugli|first1=Tony E.|title=Techniques in Protein Chemistry|date=January 1, 1989|publisher=Academic Press, Inc.|location=San Diego, CA|isbn=978-1-4832-6823-1|page=17|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zuRbAwAAQBAJ&pg=PA17|access-date=9 June 2017}}</ref> 
and the purification of reagents was improved. [[High-performance liquid chromatography|HPLC]] analysis techniques were used to reduce analysis times and extend the technique's applicable range.<ref name="Kinter"/> 
The amount of protein required for an analysis decreased, from 10-100 nanomoles for Edman and Begg's protein sequencer, to the low picomole range, a revolutionary increase in the sensitivity of the technology.<ref name="Kinter">{{cite book|last1=Kinter|first1=Michael|last2=Sherman|first2=Nicholas E.|title=Protein sequencing and identification using tandem mass spectrometry|date=2000|publisher=Wiley-Interscience|location=New York, NY|isbn=978-0-471-32249-8|pages=13–14|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1fmdXMG-72AC&pg=PA13|access-date=8 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Wittmann-Liebold">{{cite web|last1=Wittmann-Liebold|first1=Brigitte|title=Reflections on the MPSA-Conferences: Development and Innovations of Protein and Peptide Structure An alysis in the Past 30 Years|url=https://www.bnl.gov/iapsap/linkable_files/pdf/MPSA1975-2004Wittmann-Liebold-Reflections.pdf|website=MPSA|date=2005}}</ref><ref name="Gardiner"/><ref name="Hewick">{{cite journal|last1=Hewick|first1=RM|last2=Hunkapiller|first2=MW|last3=Hood|first3=LE|last4=Dreyer|first4=WJ|title=A gas-liquid solid phase peptide and protein sequenator|journal=J Biol Chem|date=August 10, 1981|volume=256|issue=15|pages=7990–7|doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)43377-7|url=http://authors.library.caltech.edu/11620/1/HEWjbc81.pdf|access-date=8 June 2017|pmid=7263636|doi-access=free}}</ref> 
The new sequencer offered significant advantages in speed and sample size compared to commercial sequencers of the time, the most popular of which were built by [[Beckman Instruments]].<ref name="García-Sancho"/> 
Commercialized as the Model 470A protein sequencer, it allowed scientists to determine partial amino acid sequences of proteins that had not previously been accessible, characterizing new proteins and better understanding their activity, function, and effects in therapeutics. These discoveries had significant ramifications in biology, medicine, and pharmacology.<ref name="Marx">{{cite book|last1=Marx|first1=Jean L.|title=A Revolution in biotechnology|date=1989|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge|isbn=978-0-521-32749-7|page=12|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=yU89JSZsS30C&pg=PA12|access-date=9 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Stephenson"/><ref name="Springer">{{cite journal|last1=Springer|first1=Mark|title=Applied Biosystems: Celebrating 25 Years of Advancing Science|journal=American Laboratory News|date=2006|volume=May|url=https://www2.appliedbiosystems.com/about/presskit/pdfs/celebrating_25_years_aln_article.pdf|access-date=9 June 2017}}</ref>

The first automated DNA synthesizer resulted from a collaboration with [[Marvin H. Caruthers]] of the [[University of Colorado Boulder]], and was based on Caruthers' work elucidating the chemistry of phosphoramidite [[oligonucleotide synthesis]].<ref name="Caruthers">{{cite journal|last1=Caruthers|first1=M. H.|title=The Chemical Synthesis of DNA/RNA: Our Gift to Science|journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry|date=6 December 2012|volume=288|issue=2|pages=1420–1427|doi=10.1074/jbc.X112.442855|pmid=23223445|pmc=3543024|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Laikhter">{{cite web|last1=Laikhter|first1=Andrei|last2=Linse|first2=Klaus D.|title=The Chemical Synthesis of Oligonucleotides|url=http://www.biosyn.com/tew/the-chemical-synthesis-of-oligonucleotides.aspx|website=Biosynthesis|access-date=9 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Hogrefe"/> 
Caltech staff scientist Suzanna J. Horvath worked with Hood and Hunkapiller to learn Caruthers' techniques in order to design a prototype that automated the repetitive steps involved in Caruthers' method for DNA synthesis.<ref name="Emery">{{cite web|last1=Emery|first1=Theo|title=Gene-mapping pioneer receive Lemelson-MIT prize|url=https://www.seacoastonline.com/story/news/2003/04/24/gene-mapping-pioneer-receive-lemelson/51273499007/|website=Associated Press|access-date=April 24, 2003}}</ref><ref name="anchem">{{cite journal|last1=Hood|first1=Lee|title=A Personal Journey of Discovery: Developing Technology and Changing Biology|journal=Annual Review of Analytical Chemistry|date=July 2008|volume=1|issue=1|pages=1–43|doi=10.1146/annurev.anchem.1.031207.113113|pmid=20636073|bibcode=2008ARAC....1....1H|doi-access=}}</ref> 
The resulting prototype was capable of forming short pieces of DNA called oligonucleotides, which could be used in DNA mapping and gene identification.<ref name="Emery"/><ref name="Stephenson"/> 
The first commercial phosphoramidite DNA synthesizer was developed from this prototype by Applied Biosystems,<ref name="Hogrefe">{{cite web|last1=Hogrefe|first1=Richard|title=A Short History of Oligonucleotide Synthesis|url=https://www.trilinkbiotech.com/tech/oligo_history.asp|website=Trilink Biotechnologies|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> 
who installed the first Model 380A in Caruthers' lab at the University of Colorado in December 1982, before beginning official commercial shipment of the new instrument.<ref name="Caruthers"/> 
Revolutionizing the field of molecular biology, the DNA synthesizer enabled biologists to synthesize DNA fragments for cloning and other genetic manipulations. Molecular biologists were able to produce DNA probes and primers for use in DNA sequencing and mapping, gene cloning, and gene synthesis. The DNA synthesizer played a critical role in the identification of many important genes and in the development of the [[polymerase chain reaction]] (PCR), the critical technique used to [[Gene duplication#Gene duplication as amplification|amplify segments of DNA]] a million-fold.<ref name="Stephenson"/><ref name="Personal"/>

The first commercial automated peptide synthesizer, sometimes referred to as a protein synthesizer, was developed by Hood and [[Stephen Kent (chemist)|Stephen B. H. Kent]], a senior research associate at Caltech from 1983 to 1989.<ref name="Chicago">{{cite web|title=Stephen Kent|url=https://chemistry.uchicago.edu/faculty/stephen-kent|website=The University of Chicago|access-date=12 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="anchem"/> The automated, programmable peptide synthesizer had previously been invented and developed by Bruce Merrifield and colleagues at Rockefeller University, and Merrifield received the Novel Prize for this invention.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://americanhistory.si.edu/collections/search/object/nmah_1450167#:~:text=Proteins%2C%20which%20are%20among%20the,into%20chains%20one%20by%20one | title=Programmer, Peptide Synthesizer }}</ref> The peptide synthesizer assembles long peptides and short proteins from amino acid subunits,<ref name="Personal"/> in quantities sufficient for subsequent analysis of their structure and function. The commercially available instrument from Applied Biosystems led to a number of significant results, including the synthesis of [[HIV-1 protease]] in a collaboration between Kent and [[Merck & Co.|Merck]] and the analysis of its crystalline structure. Based on this research, Merck developed an important antiprotease drug for the treatment of [[AIDS]]. Kent carried out a number of important synthesis and structure-function studies in Hood's lab at Caltech.<ref name="anchem"/>

Among the notable of the inventions from Hood's lab was the automated DNA sequencer. It made possible high-speed sequencing of the structure of DNA, including the human genome. It automated many of the tasks that researchers had previously done by hand.<ref name="Economist">{{cite news|title=Medicine without frontiers|newspaper=The Economist|date=September 15, 2005|url=https://www.economist.com/technology-quarterly/2005/09/17/medicine-without-frontiers|access-date=12 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Perkel">{{cite news|last1=Perkel|first1=Jeffrey|title=An Automated DNA Sequencer|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/15932/title/An-Automated-DNA-Sequencer/|access-date=12 June 2017|work=The Scientist|date=September 27, 2004}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Caltech and the Human Genome Project|url=http://www.caltech.edu/news/caltech-and-human-genome-project-406|website=Caltech News|date=June 26, 2000}}</ref> Researchers Jane Z. Sanders and [[Lloyd M. Smith]] developed a way to color code the basic [[nucleotide]] units of DNA with fluorescent tags, green for [[adenine]] (A), yellow-green for [[guanine]] (G), orange for [[cytosine]] (C) and red for [[thymine]] (T).<ref name="Mathews"/> Four differently colored [[fluorophores]], each one specific to a reaction with one of the bases, are covalently attached to the oligonucleotide primer for the enzymatic DNA sequence analysis.<ref name="Sanders"/> During the analysis, fragments are passed downwards through a gel tube, the smallest and lightest fragments passing through the gel tube first. A laser light passed through a filter wheel causes the bases to fluoresce. The resulting fluorescent colors are detected by a photomultiplier and recorded by a computer. The first DNA fragment to be sequenced was a common [[cloning vector]], [[M13 bacteriophage|M13]].<ref name="Mathews">{{cite news|last1=Mathews|first1=Jay|title=Caltech's New DNA-Analysis Machine Expected to Speed Cancer Research|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1986/06/12/caltechs-new-dna-analysis-machine-expected-to-speed-cancer-research/3acc9731-64e9-4b15-acf9-91f76615a072/|access-date=12 June 2017|newspaper=The Washington Post|date=June 12, 1986}}</ref><ref name="Fung">{{cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=L M|last2=Fung|first2=S|last3=Hunkapiller|first3=M W|last4=Hunkapiller|first4=T J|last5=Hood|first5=L E|title=The synthesis of oligonucleotides containing an aliphatic amino group at the 5' terminus: synthesis of fluorescent DNA primers for use in DNA sequence analysis|journal=Nucleic Acids Research|date=April 11, 1985|volume=13|issue=7|pages=2399–2412|doi=10.1093/nar/13.7.2399|pmc=341163|pmid=4000959}}</ref><ref name="Sanders">{{cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=Lloyd M.|last2=Sanders|first2=Jane Z.|last3=Kaiser|first3=Robert J.|last4=Hughes|first4=Peter|last5=Dodd|first5=Chris|last6=Connell|first6=Charles R.|last7=Heiner|first7=Cheryl|last8=Kent|first8=Stephen B. H.|last9=Hood|first9=Leroy E.|title=Fluorescence detection in automated DNA sequence analysis|journal=Nature|date=12 June 1986|volume=321|issue=6071|pages=674–679|doi=10.1038/321674a0|pmid=3713851|bibcode=1986Natur.321..674S|s2cid=27800972}}</ref>

The DNA sequencer was a critical technology for the [[Human Genome Project]].<ref name="Hutchison">{{cite journal|last1=Hutchison|first1=C. A.|title=DNA sequencing: bench to bedside and beyond|journal=Nucleic Acids Research|date=28 August 2007|volume=35|issue=18|pages=6227–6237|doi=10.1093/nar/gkm688|pmc=2094077|pmid=17855400}}</ref><ref name="Sanders"/> 
Hood was involved with the Human Genome Project from its first meeting, held at the [[University of California, Santa Cruz]], in 1985. Hood became an enthusiastic advocate for The Human Genome Project and its potential.<ref name=KyotoLecture2002/><ref name="MIT"/><ref name="Gannett">{{cite book|editor-last1=Zalta|editor-first1=Edward N.|title=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy|date=2012|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|location=Stanford, CA|last1=Gannett|first1=Lisa|chapter=The Human Genome Project|chapter-url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/human-genome/}}</ref><ref name="Rowen">{{cite journal|last1=Hood|first1=Leroy|last2=Rowen|first2=Lee|title=The human genome project: big science transforms biology and medicine|journal=Genome Medicine|date=2013|volume=5|issue=9|page=79|doi=10.1186/gm483|pmc=4066586|pmid=24040834 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Hood directed the Human Genome Center's sequencing of portions of human chromosomes [[Chromosome 14 (human)|14]] and [[Chromosome 14 (human)|15]].<ref name="NASAward">{{cite web|title=NAS Award for Chemistry in Service to Society|url=http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/chemistry-in-service-to-society.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120727030440/http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/chemistry-in-service-to-society.html|archive-date=July 27, 2012|website=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=4 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Brüls">{{cite journal|last1=Brüls|first1=Thomas|display-authors=etal|title=A physical map of human chromosome 14|journal=Nature|date=15 February 2001|volume=409|issue=6822|pages=947–948|doi=10.1038/35057177|pmid=11237018|bibcode=2001Natur.409..947B|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Lander">{{cite journal|last1=Lander|first1=Eric S.|display-authors=etal|title=Initial sequencing and analysis of the human genome|journal=Nature|date=15 February 2001|volume=409|issue=6822|pages=860–921|doi=10.1038/35057062|pmid=11237011|url=https://deepblue.lib.umich.edu/bitstream/2027.42/62798/1/409860a0.pdf|bibcode=2001Natur.409..860L|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Heilig">{{cite journal|last1=Heilig|first1=Roland|display-authors=etal|title=The DNA sequence and analysis of human chromosome 14|journal=Nature|date=1 January 2003|volume=421|issue=6923|pages=601–607|doi=10.1038/nature01348|pmid=12508121|bibcode=2003Natur.421..601H|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Zody">{{cite journal|last1=Zody|first1=Michael C.|display-authors=etal|title=Analysis of the DNA sequence and duplication history of human chromosome 15|journal=Nature|date=30 March 2006|volume=440|issue=7084|pages=671–675|doi=10.1038/nature04601|pmid=16572171|bibcode=2006Natur.440..671Z|doi-access=free}}</ref>

At the University of Washington in the 1990s, Hood, Alan Blanchard, and others developed ink-jet DNA synthesis technology for creating [[DNA microarrays]].<ref name="Bumgarner">{{cite book|last1=Bumgarner|first1=Roger|chapter=Overview of DNA microarrays: Types, applications, and their future|title=Nucleic Acid Arrays|series=Current Protocols in Molecular Biology|date=January 2013|volume=101|issue=1|pages=22.1.1–22.1.11|doi=10.1002/0471142727.mb2201s101|pmc=4011503|pmid=23288464|isbn=978-0-471-14272-0}}</ref><ref name="Blanchard">{{cite journal|last1=Blanchard|first1=A.P.|last2=Kaiser|first2=R.J.|last3=Hood|first3=L.E.|title=High-density oligonucleotide arrays|journal=Biosensors and Bioelectronics|date=January 1996|volume=11|issue=6–7|pages=687–690|doi=10.1016/0956-5663(96)83302-1|s2cid=13321733|url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/ef64/0e1b38e1bcbd1bf055eef7a3c41115172b49.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180313031450/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/ef64/0e1b38e1bcbd1bf055eef7a3c41115172b49.pdf|archive-date=2018-03-13|access-date=12 June 2017}}</ref> By 2004, their ink-jet DNA synthesizer supported high-throughput identification and quantification of nucleic acids through the creation of one of the first DNA array chips, with expression levels numbering tens of thousands of genes.<ref name="IEEEAward"/><ref name="Lausted"/> 
Array analysis has become a standard technique for molecular biologists who wish to monitor gene expression.<ref name="Lausted">{{cite journal|last1=Lausted|first1=Christopher|last2=Dahl|first2=Timothy|last3=Warren|first3=Charles|last4=King|first4=Kimberly|last5=Smith|first5=Kimberly|last6=Johnson|first6=Michael|last7=Saleem|first7=Ramsey|last8=Aitchison|first8=John|last9=Hood|first9=Lee|last10=Lasky|first10=Stephen R|journal=Genome Biology|title=POSaM: a fast, flexible, open-source, inkjet oligonucleotide synthesizer and microarrayer|date=2004|volume=5|issue=8|pages=R58|doi=10.1186/gb-2004-5-8-r58|pmid=15287980|pmc=507883 |doi-access=free }}</ref> 
DNA ink-jet printer technology has had a significant impact on genomics, biology, and medicine.<ref name="Kosuri">{{cite journal|last1=Kosuri|first1=Sriram|last2=Church|first2=George M|title=Large-scale de novo DNA synthesis: technologies and applications|journal=Nature Methods|date=29 April 2014|volume=11|issue=5|pages=499–507|doi=10.1038/nmeth.2918|pmid=24781323|pmc=7098426}}</ref><ref name="Zhang">{{cite magazine|last1=Zhang|first1=Sarah|title=Cheap DNA Sequencing Is Here. Writing DNA Is Next|url=https://www.wired.com/2015/11/making-dna/|access-date=12 June 2017|magazine=Wired|date=November 20, 2015}}</ref><ref name="Hwang">{{cite thesis|last1=Hwang|first1=Samuel James|title=DNA as a programmable material: de novo gene synthesis and error correction|publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology|date=2008|hdl=1721.1/44423}}</ref>

===Immunology and neurobiology===

Hood also made generative discoveries in the field of molecular [[immunology]]. His studies of the amino acid sequences of [[immunoglobulins]] (also known as antibodies) helped to fuel the 1970s' debate regarding the generation of immune diversity and supported the hypothesis advanced by [[William J. Dreyer]] that immunoglobulin (antibody) chains are encoded by two separate genes (a constant and a variable gene). He (and others) conducted pioneering studies on the structure and diversity of the antibody genes. This research led to verification of the "two genes, one polypeptide" hypothesis and insights into the mechanisms responsible for the diversification of the immunoglobulin variable genes.<ref name="Gardiner"/><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Nossal|first1=Gustav J. V.|title=The double helix and immunology|journal=Nature|date=23 January 2003|volume=421|issue=6921|pages=440–444|doi=10.1038/nature01409|pmid=12540919|bibcode=2003Natur.421..440N|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Rees">{{cite book|last1=Rees|first1=Anthony R.|title=The Antibody Molecule: From Antitoxins to Therapeutic Antibodies|date=2015|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=978-0-19-964657-9|pages=104–120|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=N0vYBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA104|access-date=12 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Davis">{{cite journal|last1=Hood|first1=L.|last2=Davis|first2=M.|last3=Early|first3=P.|last4=Calame|first4=K.|last5=Kim|first5=S.|last6=Crews|first6=S.|last7=Huang|first7=H.|title=Two types of DNA rearrangements in immunoglobulin genes|journal=Cold Spring Harbor Symposia on Quantitative Biology|date=1981|volume=45|issue=2|pages=887–898|url=https://uncch.pure.elsevier.com/en/publications/two-types-of-dna-rearrangements-in-immunoglobulin-genes|access-date=12 June 2017|doi=10.1101/sqb.1981.045.01.106|pmid=6790221|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name="revolution"/> 
Hood shared the Lasker Award in 1987 for these studies.<ref name="Lasker"/>

Additionally, Hood was among the first to study, at the gene level, the MHC (major histocompatibility complex) gene family<ref name="Goodenow">{{cite journal|last1=Hood|first1=Leroy|last2=Steinmetz|first2=Michael|last3=Goodenow|first3=Robert|title=Genes of the major histocompatibility complex|journal=Cell|date=April 1982|volume=28|issue=4|pages=685–687|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(82)90046-0|pmid=6284368|s2cid=41098069|url=http://www.cell.com/cell/pdf/0092-8674(82)90046-0.pdf|access-date=12 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="Steinmetz">{{cite journal|last1=Hood|first1=L|last2=Steinmetz|first2=M|last3=Malissen|first3=B|title=Genes of the Major Histocompatibility Complex of the Mouse|journal=Annual Review of Immunology|date=April 1983|volume=1|issue=1|pages=529–568|doi=10.1146/annurev.iy.01.040183.002525|pmid=6152713}}</ref> and the T-cell receptor gene families<ref name="Glusman">{{cite journal|last1=Glusman|first1=Gustavo|last2=Rowen|first2=Lee|last3=Lee|first3=Inyoul|last4=Boysen|first4=Cecilie|last5=Roach|first5=Jared C.|last6=Smit|first6=Arian F.A.|last7=Wang|first7=Kai|last8=Koop|first8=Ben F.|last9=Hood|first9=Leroy|title=Comparative Genomics of the Human and Mouse T Cell Receptor Loci|journal=Immunity|date=September 2001|volume=15|issue=3|pages=337–349|doi=10.1016/S1074-7613(01)00200-X|pmid=11567625|doi-access=free}}</ref> as well as being among first to demonstrate that [[Alternative splicing|alternative RNA splicing]] was a fundamental mechanism for generating alternative forms of antibodies. He showed that RNA splicing is the mechanism for generating the membrane bound and the secreted forms of antibodies.<ref name="Zhiguo">{{cite journal|last1=E|first1=Zhiguo|last2=Wang|first2=Lei|last3=Zhou|first3=Jianhua|title=Splicing and alternative splicing in rice and humans|journal=BMB Reports|date=30 September 2013|volume=46|issue=9|pages=439–447|doi=10.5483/BMBRep.2013.46.9.161|pmc=4133877|pmid=24064058}}</ref><ref name="Rogers">{{cite journal|last1=Early|first1=P|last2=Rogers|first2=J|last3=Davis|first3=M|last4=Calame|first4=K|last5=Bond|first5=M|last6=Wall|first6=R|last7=Hood|first7=L|title=Two mRNAs can be produced from a single immunoglobulin ? gene by alternative RNA processing pathways|journal=Cell|date=June 1980|volume=20|issue=2|pages=313–319|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(80)90617-0|pmid=6771020|s2cid=39580237}}</ref>

In neurobiology, Hood and his colleagues were the first to clone and study the myelin basic protein (MBP) gene. The MBP is a central component in the sheath that wraps and protects neurons.<ref name="Kamholz">{{cite journal|last1=Kamholz|first1=J|last2=Spielman|first2=R|last3=Gogolin|first3=K|last4=Modi|first4=W|last5=O'Brien|first5=S|last6=Lazzarini|first6=R|title=The human myelin-basic-protein gene: chromosomal localization and RFLP analysis|journal=Am J Hum Genet|date=1987|volume=40|issue=4|pages=365–373|pmc=1684086|pmid=2437795}}</ref><ref name="pmid2414074">{{cite journal |vauthors=Saxe DF, Takahashi N, Hood L, Simon MI | title = Localization of the human myelin basic protein gene (MBP) to region 18q22----qter by in situ hybridization | journal = Cytogenet. Cell Genet. | volume = 39 | issue = 4 | pages = 246–9 | year = 1985 | pmid = 2414074 | doi = 10.1159/000132152}}</ref> Hood demonstrated that the condition called "shiverer mouse" arose from a defect in the MBP gene. Hood's research group corrected the neurological defect in mice (the shiverer defect) by transferring a normal MBP gene into the fertilized egg of the shiverer mouse. These discoveries led to extensive studies of MBP and its biology.<ref name="Walters">{{cite book|last1=Walters|first1=LeRoy|last2=Palmer|first2=Julie Gage|title=The ethics of human gene therapy|date=1996|publisher=Oxford University Press|location=New York|isbn=978-0-19-505955-7|pages=61–62|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cJn4fJL4Q50C&pg=PA61|access-date=12 June 2017}}</ref>

===Systems biology and systems medicine===

Beginning in the 1990s, Hood focused more on cross-disciplinary biology and systems biology. He established in 1992 the first cross-disciplinary biology department, the Molecular Biotechnology Department at the [[University of Washington]].<ref name=Dietrich1992/><ref name="Herring"/> 
In 2000, he co-founded the [[Institute for Systems Biology]] (ISB) in Seattle, Washington to develop strategies and technologies for systems approaches to biology and medicine.<ref name="ISB"/><ref name="Pollack"/><ref name="Vermeulen"/> He co-led the Hood-Price research lab at ISB with [[Nathan D. Price|Nathan Price]] until Price left to join Center for Human Healthspan at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging.

Hood pioneered the [[systems biology]] concept of considering human biology as a "network of networks."<ref name="Rodbell">{{cite web|title=Hood Delivers Rodbell Lecture, Mar. 10|url=https://nihrecord.nih.gov/newsletters/2015/02_27_2015/story7.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150522051727/http://nihrecord.nih.gov/newsletters/2015/02_27_2015/story7.htm|archive-date=May 22, 2015|website=NIH Record|publisher=National Institutes of Health|access-date=12 June 2017}}</ref><ref name="AYOGO">{{cite news|title=Life Science Innovation in Seattle is at the Top of its Game|url=http://ayogo.com/blog/life-science-innovation/|access-date=12 June 2017|work=AYOGO|date=June 14, 2016}}</ref> In this model, understanding how systems function requires knowledge of: (1) the components of each network (including genetic, molecular, cellular, organ networks), (2) how these networks inter- and intra-connect, (3) how the networks change over time and undergo perturbations, and (4) how function is achieved within these networks.<ref name="Nass">{{cite book|editor-last1=Nass|editor-first1=Sharyl J.|editor-last2=Wizemann|editor-first2=Theresa|title=INFORMATICS NEEDS AND CHALLENGES IN CANCER RESEARCH Workshop Summary|date=2012|publisher=NATIONAL ACADEMIES PRESS|location=Washington, D.C.|chapter=Chapter 3: Informatics and Personalized Medicine|pages=31–42|doi=10.17226/13425 |pmid=24901181 |isbn=978-0-309-25948-4 |chapter-url=https://www.nap.edu/read/13425/chapter/4#41|access-date=12 June 2017 |author1=National Cancer Policy Forum |author2=Board on Health Care Services |author3=Institute of Medicine }}</ref> At the ISB under Hood's direction, genomic, transcriptomic, metabolomic and proteomic technologies are used to understand the "network of networks" and are focused on diverse biological systems<ref name="Wang">{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Daojing|last2=Bodovitz|first2=Steven|title=Single cell analysis: the new frontier in ?omics?|journal=Trends in Biotechnology|date=June 2010|volume=28|issue=6|pages=281–290|doi=10.1016/j.tibtech.2010.03.002|pmc=2876223|pmid=20434785}}</ref> 
(e.g. yeast, mice and humans).<ref name="Koop">{{cite journal|last1=Hood|first1=Leroy|last2=Koop|first2=Ben|last3=Goverman|first3=Joan|last4=Hunkapiller|first4=Tim|title=Model genomes: The benefits of analysing homologous human and mouse sequences|journal=Trends in Biotechnology|date=1992|volume=10|issue=1–2|pages=19–22|doi=10.1016/0167-7799(92)90161-N|pmid=1367926}}</ref>

Hood applies the notion of systems biology to the study of medicine,<ref name="Wolkenhauer">{{cite journal|last1=Wolkenhauer|first1=Olaf|last2=Auffray|first2=Charles|last3=Jaster|first3=Robert|last4=Steinhoff|first4=Gustav|last5=Dammann|first5=Olaf|title=The road from systems biology to systems medicine|journal=Pediatric Research|date=11 January 2013|volume=73|issue=4–2|pages=502–507|doi=10.1038/pr.2013.4|pmid=23314297|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="Auffray">{{cite journal|last1=Auffray|first1=Charles|last2=Chen|first2=Zhu|last3=Hood|first3=Leroy|title=Systems medicine: the future of medical genomics and healthcare|journal=Genome Medicine|date=2009|volume=1|issue=1|page=2|doi=10.1186/gm2|pmid=19348689|pmc=2651587 |doi-access=free }}</ref> specifically to cancer<ref name="Tian">{{cite journal|last1=Tian|first1=Q.|last2=Price|first2=N. D.|last3=Hood|first3=L.|title=Systems cancer medicine: towards realization of predictive, preventive, personalized and participatory (P4) medicine|journal=Journal of Internal Medicine|date=February 2012|volume=271|issue=2|pages=111–121|doi=10.1111/j.1365-2796.2011.02498.x|pmid=22142401|pmc=3978383}}</ref> and [[neurodegenerative disease]].<ref name="Zhou">{{cite journal|last1=Lausted|first1=Christopher|last2=Lee|first2=Inyoul|last3=Zhou|first3=Yong|last4=Qin|first4=Shizhen|last5=Sung|first5=Jaeyun|last6=Price|first6=Nathan D.|last7=Hood|first7=Leroy|last8=Wang|first8=Kai|title=Systems Approach to Neurodegenerative Disease Biomarker Discovery|journal=Annual Review of Pharmacology and Toxicology|date=6 January 2014|volume=54|issue=1|pages=457–481|doi=10.1146/annurev-pharmtox-011613-135928|pmid=24160693|doi-access=free}}</ref> His [[research article]] on a systems approach to [[Transmissible spongiform encephalopathy|prion diseases]] in 2009 was one of the first to thoroughly explore the use of systems biology to interrogate the dynamic network changes in disease models. These studies are the first to explain the dynamics of diseased-perturbed networks and have expanded to include frontal temporal [[dementia]] and [[Huntington's disease]].<ref name="Omenn">{{cite journal|last1=Omenn|first1=Gilbert S|title=A landmark systems analysis of prion disease of the brain|journal=Molecular Systems Biology|date=24 March 2009|volume=5|page=254|doi=10.1038/msb.2009.12|pmc=2671917|pmid=19308093}}</ref><ref name="Daehee">{{cite journal|last1=Hwang|first1=Daehee|last2=Lee|first2=Inyoul Y|last3=Yoo|first3=Hyuntae|last4=Gehlenborg|first4=Nils|last5=Cho|first5=Ji-Hoon|last6=Petritis|first6=Brianne|last7=Baxter|first7=David|last8=Pitstick|first8=Rose|last9=Young|first9=Rebecca|last10=Spicer|first10=Doug|last11=Price|first11=Nathan D|last12=Hohmann|first12=John G|last13=DeArmond|first13=Stephen J|last14=Carlson|first14=George A|last15=Hood|first15=Leroy E|title=A systems approach to prion disease|journal=Molecular Systems Biology|date=24 March 2009|volume=5|page=252|doi=10.1038/msb.2009.10|pmid=19308092|pmc=2671916}}</ref> 
Hood is also studying [[glioblastoma]] in mice and humans from the systems viewpoint.<ref name="Ghosh">{{cite journal|last1=Ghosh|first1=Dhimankrishna|last2=Funk|first2=Cory C.|last3=Caballero|first3=Juan|last4=Shah|first4=Nameeta|last5=Rouleau|first5=Katherine|last6=Earls|first6=John C.|last7=Soroceanu|first7=Liliana|last8=Foltz|first8=Greg|last9=Cobbs|first9=Charles S.|last10=Price|first10=Nathan D.|last11=Hood|first11=Leroy|title=A Cell-Surface Membrane Protein Signature for Glioblastoma|journal=Cell Systems|date=May 2017|volume=4|issue=5|pages=516–529.e7|doi=10.1016/j.cels.2017.03.004|pmid=28365151|pmc=5512565}}</ref>

Hood advocates several practices in the burgeoning field of [[systems medicine]], including: 
(1) The use of family genome sequencing, integrating genetics and genomics, to identify genetic variants associated with health and disease<ref name="Roach">{{cite journal|last1=Roach|first1=J. C.|last2=Glusman|first2=G.|last3=Smit|first3=A. F. A.|last4=Huff|first4=C. D.|last5=Hubley|first5=R.|last6=Shannon|first6=P. T.|last7=Rowen|first7=L.|last8=Pant|first8=K. P.|last9=Goodman|first9=N.|last10=Bamshad|first10=M.|last11=Shendure|first11=J.|last12=Drmanac|first12=R.|last13=Jorde|first13=L. B.|last14=Hood|first14=L.|last15=Galas|first15=D. J.|title=Analysis of Genetic Inheritance in a Family Quartet by Whole-Genome Sequencing|journal=Science|date=10 March 2010|volume=328|issue=5978|pages=636–639|doi=10.1126/science.1186802|pmid=20220176|pmc=3037280|bibcode=2010Sci...328..636R}}</ref>
(2) The use of targeted proteomics and biomarkers as a window into health and disease.<ref name="Mustafa">{{cite journal|last1=Mustafa|first1=Gul M|title=Targeted proteomics for biomarker discovery and validation of hepatocellular carcinoma in hepatitis C infected patients|journal=World Journal of Hepatology|date=2015|volume=7|issue=10|pages=1312–24|doi=10.4254/wjh.v7.i10.1312|pmc=4450195|pmid=26052377 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="Veenstra">{{cite journal|last1=Veenstra|first1=T. D.|title=Biomarkers: Mining the Biofluid Proteome|journal=Molecular & Cellular Proteomics|date=25 January 2005|volume=4|issue=4|pages=409–418|doi=10.1074/mcp.M500006-MCP200|pmid=15684407|doi-access=free}}</ref> He has pioneered the discovery of biomarker panels for [[lung cancer]]<ref name="Zeng">{{cite journal|last1=Zeng|first1=Xuemei|last2=Hood|first2=Brian L.|last3=Sun|first3=Mai|last4=Conrads|first4=Thomas P.|last5=Day|first5=Roger S.|last6=Weissfeld|first6=Joel L.|last7=Siegfried|first7=Jill M.|last8=Bigbee|first8=William L.|title=Lung Cancer Serum Biomarker Discovery Using Glycoprotein Capture and Liquid Chromatography Mass Spectrometry|journal=Journal of Proteome Research|date=3 December 2010|volume=9|issue=12|pages=6440–6449|doi=10.1021/pr100696n|pmid=20931982|pmc=3184639}}</ref> and [[posttraumatic stress syndrome]].<ref name="Australian">{{cite web|title='Decoding DNA: The Future of DNA Sequencing': Dr. Lee Hood Appears on Australian Radio Show|url=https://www.systemsbiology.org/news/2014/02/27/decoding-dna-the-future-of-dna-sequencing-dr-lee-hood-appears-on-australian-radio-show/|website=Institute for Systems Biology|access-date=13 June 2017|date=2014-02-28}}</ref> 
(3) The use of systems biology to stratify disease into its different subtypes allowing for more effective treatment.<ref name="Brogaard">{{cite journal|last1=Flores|first1=Mauricio|last2=Glusman|first2=Gustavo|last3=Brogaard|first3=Kristin|last4=Price|first4=Nathan D|last5=Hood|first5=Leroy|title=P4 medicine: how systems medicine will transform the healthcare sector and society|journal=Personalized Medicine|date=August 2013|volume=10|issue=6|pages=565–576|doi=10.2217/PME.13.57|pmc=4204402|pmid=25342952}}</ref><ref name="revolution"/> 
(4) The use of systems strategies to identify new types of drug targets to facilitate and accelerate the drug discovery process.<ref name="Tian"/>

=== P4 medicine ===
Since 2002 Hood has progressively expanded his vision of the future of medicine: first focusing on predictive and preventive (2P) Medicine; then predictive, preventive and personalized (3P) Medicine; and finally predictive, preventive, personalized and participatory, also known as P4 Medicine.<ref name="Chase">{{cite web|last1=Chase|first1=Dave|title=Tampa Stakes Its Claim to Lead Healthcare into the Future|url=https://thedoctorweighsin.com/tampa-stakes-its-claim-to-lead-healthcare-into-the-future/|website=The Doctor Weighs In|access-date=May 21, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140901044541/http://www.thedoctorweighsin.com/tampa-stakes-its-claim-to-lead-healthcare-into-the-future/|archive-date=September 1, 2014}}</ref> Hood states that P4 Medicine is the convergence of systems medicine, big data and patient (consumer) driven healthcare and social networks.<ref name="Brogaard"/>

Hood envisions that by the mid-2020s each individual will be surrounded by a virtual cloud of billions of data points and will have the computational tools to analyze this data and produce simple approaches to optimize wellness and minimize disease for each individual.<ref name="Flores"/><ref name="Rowen"/><ref name="revolution"/> According to this view, the patient's demand for better healthcare will be the real driving force for the acceptance of P4 Medicine by the medical community.  This driving force is exemplified by the movement known as the [[quantified self]], which uses digital devices to monitor self-parameters such as weight, activity, sleep, diet, etc.  His view is that P4 Medicine will transform the practice of medicine over the next decade, moving it from a largely reactive, disease-care approach to a proactive P4 approach that is predictive, preventive, personalized and participatory.<ref name="Brogaard"/>

In 2010, Hood co-founded the P4 Medicine institute (P4Mi), for the development of Predictive, Preventive, Personalized and Participatory (P4) Medicine.<ref name="Kirk"/> In 2021 Hood founded Phenome Health, a non profit focused on implementing his vision. He argues that P4 Medicine will improve healthcare, decrease its cost and promote innovation.<ref name="Strickland">{{cite journal|last1=Strickland|first1=Eliza|title=Medicine's Next Big Mission: Understanding Wellness|journal=IEEE Spectrum|date=29 August 2014|url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/medicines-next-big-mission-understanding-wellness|access-date=1 June 2017}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
[[File:Leroy Hood podium PITT2008.JPG|thumb|right| Leroy Hood, 2008 Pittcon Heritage Award recipient]]
[[File:Dr. Lee Hood receiving the National Medal of Science from President Obama.jpg|alt=Dr. Lee Hood receiving the National Medal of Science from President Obama|thumb|Dr. Lee Hood receiving the National Medal of Science from President Obama]]
Leroy Hood is a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] (NAS, 1982),<ref>{{cite web|title=Leroy E. Hood|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/leroy-e-hood-dyjnqz/|website=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> 
the [[National Academy of Engineering]] (2007),<ref>{{cite web|title=Dr. Leroy Hood|url=https://www.nae.edu/MembersSection/MemberDirectory/29183.aspx|website=National Academy of Engineering|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> 
the [[National Academy of Medicine]] (formerly the Institute of Medicine, 2003),<ref>{{cite web|title=National Academy of Medicine|url=https://www.washington.edu/research/honors-and-awards/national-academy-of-medicine-formerly-institute-of-medicine/|website=University of Washington|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> 
and the [[National Academy of Inventors]] (2012).<ref>{{cite web |title=Fellows List |url=https://academyofinventors.org/fellows-list/ |website=National Academy of Inventors |access-date=13 June 2022}}</ref> 
He is one of only 15 scientists ever elected to all three national academies.<ref name=ISB2004/> He is also 
a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (1982),<ref>{{cite web|title=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|url=https://www.washington.edu/research/honors-and-awards/american-academy-of-arts-and-sciences/|website=University of Washington|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> 
a member of the [[American Philosophical Society]] (2000),<ref>{{cite web|title=American Philosophical Society|url=https://www.washington.edu/research/honors-and-awards/american-philosophical-society/|website=University of Washington|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> 
a fellow of the [[American Society for Microbiology]],<ref>{{cite web|title=ASM News|url=https://www.asm.org/index.php/component/content/article/114-unknown/unknown/3164-asm-news33|website=American Society for Microbiology|access-date=2 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121111041155/http://www.asm.org/index.php/component/content/article/114-unknown/unknown/3164-asm-news33|archive-date=11 November 2012}}</ref> and a charter fellow of the [[National Academy of Inventors]] (2012).<ref>{{cite web|title=National Academy of Inventors 2012 Charter Fellow: Dr. Lee Hood|url=https://www.systemsbiology.org/news/2012/12/18/national-academy-of-inventors-2012-charter-fellow-dr-lee-hood/|website=ISB News|access-date=2 June 2017|date=2012-12-18}}</ref>
<ref name="USF">{{cite news|title=National Academy of Inventors congratulates NAI Fellows Robert Langer and Leroy Hood, and NAI Member James Wynne on receiving U.S. National Medals|url=http://www.research.usf.edu/absolute-news/templates/usfri-template.aspx?articleid=866&zoneid=1|access-date=2 June 2017|work=USF Research News|agency=University of South Florida|date=January 8, 2013|archive-date=4 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200704180106/http://www.research.usf.edu/absolute-news/templates/usfri-template.aspx?articleid=866&zoneid=1}}</ref> 
He has received 17 honorary degrees<ref name="ISB"/> from institutions including Johns Hopkins<ref>{{cite web|title=Honorary Degrees Awarded|url=https://commencement.jhu.edu/our-history/honorary-degrees-awarded/|website=Johns Hopkins University|access-date=2 June 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180221112951/https://commencement.jhu.edu/our-history/honorary-degrees-awarded/|archive-date=21 February 2018}}</ref> and [[Yale University]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Honorary Degree Citations Commencement 2009|url=http://news.yale.edu/2009/05/25/honorary-degree-citations-commencement-2009|access-date=2 June 2017|work=Yale News|date=May 25, 2009}}</ref>

In 1987 Hood shared the [[Albert Lasker Award for Basic Medical Research]] with [[Philip Leder]] and [[Susumu Tonegawa]] for studies of the mechanism of immune diversity.<ref name="Lasker">{{cite web|title=1987 Albert Lasker Basic Medical Research Award Genetic basis of antibody diversity|url=http://www.laskerfoundation.org/awards/show/genetic-basis-of-antibody-diversity/|website=Albert And Mary Lasker Foundation built by blenderbox|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> 
He subsequently was awarded the [[Dickson Prize]] in 1988.<ref name="Dickson">{{cite web|title=Dickson Prize: Past Winners|url=http://www.cmu.edu/dickson-prize/past-winners/index.html|website=Carnegie Mellon University|access-date=2 June 2017}}</ref> In 1987, Hood also received the Golden Plate Award of the [[Academy of Achievement|American Academy of Achievement]].<ref>{{cite web|title= Golden Plate Awardees of the American Academy of Achievement |website=www.achievement.org|publisher=[[American Academy of Achievement]]|url=https://achievement.org/our-history/golden-plate-awards/#science-exploration}}</ref>

He won the 2002 [[Kyoto Prize]] for Advanced Technology for developing automated technologies for analyzing proteins and genes;<ref name="Kyoto"/> 
the 2003 [[Lemelson-MIT Prize]] for Innovation and Invention for inventing "four instruments that have unlocked much of the mystery of human biology" by helping decode the [[genome]];<ref name="Lemelson">{{cite web|title=Leroy Hood|url=http://lemelson.mit.edu/winners/leroy-hood-0|website=Lemelson-MIT Program|access-date=1 December 2016|archive-date=4 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200704232004/https://lemelson.mit.edu/winners/leroy-hood-0}}</ref> 
the 2004 [[Biotechnology Heritage Award]];<ref name=CHFBio>{{cite web|title= Biotechnology Heritage Award|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/biotechnology-heritage-award|website=[[Science History Institute]]|access-date=21 February 2018|date=2016-05-31}}</ref><ref name="Biotech">{{cite news|title=Leroy Hood to receive 2004 Biotechnology Heritage Award|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2004-05/chf-lht052604.php|access-date=1 June 2017|work=Eureka Alert|date=May 26, 2004}}</ref> the 2004 [[Association for Molecular Pathology]] Award for Excellence in Molecular Diagnostics<ref>{{Cite web |title=Past Recipients |url=https://www.amp.org/membership/awards-grants-honors/amp-award-for-excellence-in-molecular-diagnostics/past-recipients/ |access-date=2023-03-03 |website=Association for Molecular Pathology |language=en}}</ref> 
the 2006 [[Heinz Award]] in Technology, the Economy and Employment,<ref name="Heinz">{{cite web|title=Dr. Leroy Hood|url=http://heinzawards.net/recipients/leroy-hood|website=The Heinz Awards|access-date=1 December 2016}}</ref> for breakthroughs in biomedical science on the genetic level; 
inclusion in the 2007 Inventors Hall of Fame for the automated DNA sequencer;<ref name="NIHF">{{cite news|author=National Inventors Hall of Fame|title=National Inventors Hall of Fame announces 2007 inductees|url=https://www.eurekalert.org/pub_releases/2007-02/niho-nih020807.php|access-date=1 June 2017|work=Eureka Alert|date=February 8, 2007}}</ref> 
the 2008 [[Pittcon Heritage Award]] for helping to transform the biotechnology industry;<ref name="CHFPittcon">{{cite web|title=Pittcon Heritage Award|url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/pittcon-heritage-award|website=[[Science History Institute]]|access-date=21 February 2018|date=2016-05-31}}</ref><ref name="CENPittcon">{{cite journal|last1=Wang|first1=Linda|title=Pittcon Awards 2008|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|date=March 24, 2008|volume=86|issue=12|pages=67–68|url=http://cen.acs.org/articles/86/i12/Pittcon-Awards-2008.html|access-date=1 June 2017}}</ref> and 
the 2010 [[Kistler Prize]] for contributions to genetics that have increased knowledge of the human genome and its relationship to society.<ref name="Kistler">{{cite web|title=Foundation For the Future to Award $100,000 Kistler Prize to Dr. Leroy Hood Five Inventions Laid Technological Foundation for Genomics and Proteomics|url=http://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20100506005648/en/Foundation-Future-Award-100000-Kistler-Prize-Dr.|website=BusinessWire|date=May 6, 2010}}</ref> 
Leroy Hood won the 2011 [[Russ Prize|Fritz J. and Dolores H. Russ Prize]] "for automating DNA sequencing that revolutionized biomedicine and forensic science";<ref name="NAERuss">{{cite web|title=Fritz J. and Dolores H. Russ Prize|url=https://www.nae.edu/Projects/Awards/RussPrize/RussWinners/55323.aspx|website=National Academy of Engineering|access-date=1 June 2017}}</ref> 
the 2011 [[National Medal of Science]], presented at a White House ceremony by President Obama in early 2013;<ref name="NSF2011">{{cite web|title=The President's National Medal of Science: Recipient Details|url=https://nsf.gov/od/nms/recip_details.jsp;jsessionid=39236BA4D97AC00CC07044696EE22CE6?recip_id=5300000000480|website=National Science Foundation|access-date=1 June 2017}}</ref> 
the [[IEEE Medal for Innovations in Healthcare Technology]] in 2014,<ref name="IEEEAward">{{cite web|title=IEEE Medal for Innovations in Healthcare Technology Recipients|url=https://www.ieee.org/about/awards/bios/healthcare_recipients.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100619225202/http://ieee.org/about/awards/bios/healthcare_recipients.html|archive-date=June 19, 2010|website=IEEE|access-date=1 June 2017}}</ref> and 
the 2016 [[Ellis Island Medal of Honor]].<ref name=ISB2004>{{cite news|title=Dr. Lee Hood Receives Ellis Island Medal of Honor |url=https://www.systemsbiology.org/news/2016/05/09/dr-lee-hood-receives-ellis-island-medal-honor/|access-date=1 December 2016|publisher=Institute for Systems Biology|date=21 April 2004}}</ref> 
In 2017 he received the [[NAS Award for Chemistry in Service to Society]].<ref name="NAS2017">{{cite web|title=2017 NAS Award for Chemistry in Service to Society Leroy E. Hood|url=http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/2017/Leroy-Hood.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170130000355/http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/2017/Leroy-Hood.html|archive-date=January 30, 2017|website=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=1 June 2017}}</ref> In 2019 Hood was awarded the [[IRI Medal]], established by the Industrial Research Institute (IRI).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Awards - Best Practices in Digital Innovation|url=https://www.iriweb.org/about/awards/|access-date=2023-02-10|website=Innovation Research Interchange|language=en-US}}</ref>
